newsitem.title: PERU: Vatican mediator urges forgiveness in Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Vatican mediator urges forgiveness in Peru crisis.

text.p: The Vatican mediator in Peru's hostage crisis on Wednesday asked all parties to set aside hatred and forgive one another as a way to end the agonizing 92-day siege at the Japanese ambassador's home.
"If excesses have been committed, this is the time to forgive," Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani told reporters as he left a mass in the highland city of Ayacucho.
"Let's forget hate, rancour, revenge. Let's forget about a confrontation between winners and losers, about turning this human situation into a political discussion."

Face-to-face talks between Peru's government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), which stormed the residence on Dec. 17, are stalled with no end in sight to the ordeal of the rebels' 72 VIP captives.

Archbishop of the violence-torn Ayacucho region, Cipriani is the Vatican's representative on a three-man guarantors' commission overseeing talks aimed at finding a peaceful end to the Lima hostage crisis.
Pope John Paul II, in masses at the Vatican, has frequently made reference to the Lima siege, expressing concern for the fate of the hostages and calling for a prompt, peaceful solution.
Cipriani, whose fellow guarantors are Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Canada's ambassador Anthony Vincent, called on both sides on Tuedsay to seek a solution that upholds "human dignity."
"This is the time to understand that there is a margin for a peaceful solution but it is attainable only through pardon and reconciliation," he said.

The MRTA's main demand is freedom for some 450 imprisoned comrades, who rebels claim are enduring "inhuman" conditions in Peru's maximum security jails. President Alberto Fujimori, a close friend of Cipriani, has rejected the idea but suggested he may make other concessions, such as improving prison conditions and allowing hostage-takers to seek asylum abroad.
Cipriani, referring to prisoners, hostages, rebels and families involved, said guerrillas and the government should seek "a dignified solution to this crisis."
"That does not mean leaving vulnerable the legal system but rather accepting the dignity and right that all people have to a more dignified treatment," he said.
